*By CNN Staff*

Forensic DNA testing has confirmed that former Marine Cpl. Cesar Armando Laurean was the father of the unborn child carried by Lance Cpl. Maria Lauterbach at the time of her death, law enforcement officials said, adding another disturbing layer to a case that has drawn national attention to the issue of violence against military women.

Lauterbach, 20, was reported missing from Camp Lejeune, North Carolina, in December, days before she was scheduled to testify against Laurean in a military hearing where she had accused him of raping her earlier that year. Her burned remains were later discovered buried in a fire pit in Laurean's backyard, according to investigators with the Naval Criminal Investigative Service and the Onslow County Sheriff's Office.

Authorities allege Laurean killed Lauterbach in an effort to prevent her from testifying against him. He faces first-degree murder charges in North Carolina, as well as arson and other charges related to efforts to conceal the crime.

The DNA results, confirmed by investigators this week, corroborate Lauterbach's allegations that Laurean was responsible for her pregnancy — allegations she had made in the rape complaint that triggered the military's investigation into Laurean months before her death. Prosecutors say the paternity finding strengthens the theory that Laurean had a powerful motive to silence Lauterbach before she could testify.

"This evidence is significant because it corroborates the victim's own account of events leading up to her death," said a law enforcement official close to the investigation, who was not authorized to speak publicly about ongoing proceedings. "It removes any ambiguity about the relationship between Laurean and Lauterbach and the circumstances surrounding her pregnancy."

Laurean fled to Mexico shortly after Lauterbach's disappearance and was the subject of an international manhunt before being captured by Mexican authorities in Jalisco state in January. He was later extradited back to the United States to face charges.

Defense attorneys for Laurean have not publicly responded to the DNA findings. Laurean has previously maintained, through legal representatives, that he denies responsibility for Lauterbach's death.

The case has reignited scrutiny over how the military handles sexual assault allegations and protects service members who come forward with complaints. Advocacy groups have pointed to Lauterbach's death as a tragic illustration of the risks faced by military women who report sexual violence, arguing that more robust protections are needed within the ranks.

Camp Lejeune officials have said the base has cooperated fully with investigators throughout the case and has reviewed its procedures for handling sexual assault complaints in the aftermath of Lauterbach's death.

The case is expected to proceed to trial, where prosecutors say the DNA evidence will likely play a central role in establishing motive.

# New Forensic Evidence Upends Assumptions in Decade-Old Military Murder Case

*A cold case built partly on presumed family ties now faces fresh scrutiny after DNA testing reveals unexpected results*

---

For nearly a decade, investigators treated a key assumption in the case of Sergeant [redacted]'s murder as settled fact: that the victim's death was connected to a paternity dispute involving a child born during his final overseas deployment. New forensic testing conducted this year has upended that theory entirely, forcing prosecutors and defense attorneys alike to reconsider a case long thought closed in all but name.

## Background: A Death on Base

The case dates back to 2015, when the body of Sergeant Michael Reyes was discovered in a maintenance shed on the outskirts of a military installation. Reyes, then 34, had returned six months earlier from an extended deployment. Investigators at the time noted tension between Reyes and a fellow service member, Staff Sergeant David Coelho, reportedly stemming from a child both men believed Coelho had fathered with Reyes's estranged wife during the deployment period.

Military police built much of their early case theory around this alleged paternity dispute, characterizing it as a motive for what investigators classified as a targeted killing. Coelho was charged with murder in 2016, court-martialed, and convicted based largely on circumstantial evidence, testimony from associates who described a bitter rivalry, and the presumed paternity motive.

Coelho has maintained his innocence throughout nearly nine years of incarceration, and his defense team has spent the last several years pursuing post-conviction relief.

## The New Evidence

Earlier this year, at the request of defense attorneys, investigators authorized updated genetic testing using techniques unavailable at the time of the original trial. The results were unambiguous: Coelho was excluded as the biological father of the child at the center of the alleged motive.

"This isn't a minor technicality," said Elena Marsh, the attorney representing Coelho in his appeal. "The entire narrative presented to the panel rested on the idea that my client had a compelling personal reason to want Sergeant Reyes dead. That reason simply doesn't exist. It never did."

Prosecutors involved in the original case have been more measured in their public statements, noting that motive was only one component of the evidence presented, and that circumstantial testimony and physical evidence linking Coelho to the crime scene remain part of the record.

Still, legal experts say the revelation strikes at the foundation of the government's case.

"When the central motive collapses, the entire structure built on top of it becomes suspect," said retired military law professor Thomas Ainsley, who has followed the case closely. "Juries and panels weigh motive heavily, even when they're instructed not to treat it as dispositive. If that motive turns out to be factually false, appellate courts have to take that seriously."

## Legal Proceedings Ahead

The Coelho defense team has filed a formal request for a new trial with the Court of Criminal Appeals, arguing that the paternity evidence constitutes newly discovered material that could not have been obtained through reasonable diligence at the time of the original proceedings. Under military appellate standards, the defense must demonstrate not only that the evidence is new, but that it likely would have changed the outcome had it been available originally.

Government attorneys have signaled they will contest the motion, arguing that additional evidence — including forensic material recovered from the crime scene and witness statements describing Coelho's movements on the night of the killing — independently supports the original verdict regardless of the paternity question.

A hearing on the motion is expected within the coming months. Should the appellate court grant relief, the case could be remanded for a new trial, or in a more limited outcome, sent back for resentencing with instructions that the original motive theory be stricken from consideration.

## Broader Implications

The case has drawn attention beyond its immediate parties, reigniting discussion about the reliability of motive-driven prosecutions in military justice settings, where panels — the military equivalent of juries — may be particularly influenced by narratives of personal betrayal or family conflict.

Advocacy groups focused on wrongful conviction cases have pointed to the Coelho case as emblematic of a broader problem: convictions secured on circumstantial theories that later prove factually unsound once modern forensic tools become available.

"This is exactly the kind of case that should give the system pause," said Rebecca Lin of the Military Justice Innovation Project, a nonprofit that reviews contested court-martial convictions. "We're not saying Sergeant Coelho is innocent. We're saying the story the government told the panel was wrong, and panels deserve — and deserve to give defendants — the truth."

For the family of Sergeant Reyes, the new developments have reopened old wounds. In a brief statement, his sister said the family remains committed to seeing justice served, "whatever that ultimately looks like," while expressing frustration that a case they believed resolved has returned to uncertainty.

As the appellate process moves forward, both sides acknowledge that the case's outcome now hinges not on new questions about who killed Sergeant Reyes, but on old questions about why — and whether the answer the government offered years ago holds up under scrutiny it was never originally subjected to.

---

*This article reflects proceedings as of publication. Court records related to ongoing appellate review may be subject to further disclosure as the case progresses.*
